amstar2_items.justification: No PICO structure is used; eligibility criteria (Table 2, Box 1) specify a Canadian Indigenous context, water focus, empirical data, and integrative Indigenous-Western knowledge processes rather than PICO population, intervention, comparator, and outcomes.

No registered or published protocol is cited, no risk-of-bias assessment plan was pre-specified, and formal protocol deviations are not tracked, although inclusion criteria and reflective questions were co-developed with a National Advisory Committee and at a 2014 Water Gathering and an updated search to August 2015 was added at the NAC's direction.

Authors explicitly explain including empirical peer-reviewed studies as well as grey literature (theses, dissertations, government and NGO reports) to capture contemporary integrative water research and management practices in Canada beyond conventional academic outlets (p. 5, Box 1).

Authors searched three academic databases/aggregators (Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar) plus grey-literature databases/websites (Library and Archives Canada, Canadian Public Policy Collection, Government of Canada Publications, Google, agency websites), consulted a librarian and NAC experts, and printed search strings (Table 1); however, they restricted inclusion to English-only without methodological justification (acknowledging French exclusion as a key limitation on p. 24) and did not report backward citation/reference-list searching.
Citations from Scopus and Web of Science were screened in two stages (title/abstract then full text) by two independent reviewers, with disagreements resolved through team consensus meetings (p. 5).

Data extraction was not performed in duplicate; instead, the included literature was partitioned into four groups (First Nations, Inuit, Metis, and multi-site contexts) and coded across three team members using the 33-question SRR Reporting Tool without duplicate independent extraction or inter-rater reliability checks (p. 7).
Only aggregate exclusion counts are reported in the Findings text (p. 13; Figure 1 is blank in the PDF), and no list of full-text excluded studies with individual exclusion reasons is provided.
No characteristics-of-included-studies table or complete list of the 63 included documents is provided; results are reported only as aggregate descriptive statistics and selective narrative examples.
No risk-of-bias or methodological quality appraisal of individual included primary studies or grey-literature reports was conducted.

Although 'Funding agency' is listed as Variable 12 in the extraction Reporting Tool (Table 3, p. 9) and p. 22 briefly notes a dearth of science/engineering funding, funding sources of individual included studies are never reported.
No quantitative meta-analysis was conducted; the review presents descriptive counts and qualitative realist thematic synthesis.
Study-level risk of bias or methodological quality was neither assessed nor accounted for when interpreting and discussing findings.

Authors discuss substantive contextual, regional, and disciplinary variation across included records, including differences between social science vs. engineering/natural science studies, treaty vs. non-treaty/land-claim contexts (e.g., British Columbia vs. northern territories), and drinking water vs. broader environmental/ice contexts.

Funding from the Canadian Water Network is acknowledged (p. 2), but there is no conflict-of-interest disclosure or management statement, even though several co-authors' own primary studies (e.g., Daley et al. 2014, Harper et al. 2011, Martin et al. 2007) are included in the review.

raw_response.methodological_notes: 1. Hybrid Design & AMSTAR 2 Fit: Castleden et al. (2017) describe their study as a combined 'systematic and realist review (SRR)' examining the 'extent, range, and nature' of academic and grey literature on integrative Indigenous and Western knowledge approaches to water research and management in Canada (1979–Aug 2015), using a 33-item Context-Mechanism-Outcome reporting tool co-created with a National Advisory Committee and Water Gathering participants. AMSTAR 2 is borderline for this scoping/realist hybrid, and the review scores Critically Low due to lack of a registered protocol, exclusion of French-language Canadian literature without methodological justification, non-duplicate partitioned extraction, no list of excluded studies, no table of included studies, no risk-of-bias/quality assessment, and no conflict-of-interest statement (despite co-authors' own primary studies—Daley 2014, Harper 2011, Martin 2007—being included). 2. Screening Flow Discrepancies: Figure 1 is blank in the published PDF, and the narrative screening numbers on p. 13 do not reconcile cleanly (226 academic records retrieved -> 29 included + 37 excluded + 36 full-text reviewed = 102 accounted for, followed by 'a total of 40 included; 64 excluded' = 104; plus 53 grey-literature documents yielding 12 reports and 11 theses/dissertations, for a reported total of 279 reviewed and 63 included). 3. Incomplete Identification of Included Studies: No included-studies table, appendix, or bibliography marker is printed; 57 of the 63 included records are identifiable via inline citations in Findings (pp. 16–21), whereas several Canadian water papers in the Reference list (e.g., Basdeo & Bharadwaj 2013, Mascarenhas 2007, Phare 2011, Sanderson et al. 2015, Walkem 2007) appear only in the Introduction or Discussion and cannot be verified as formally included. Note also that the printed DOI for Gearheard et al. (2006) on p. 29 ('10.3390/ijerph13050505') is a copy-paste error duplicating Galway (2016). 4. Narrow Criterion 2 Fit: Borderline—only 26% of included studies focused on drinking water and ~14 examined water governance, treaty/Aboriginal water rights, operator certification, or First Nations drinking-water legislative frameworks, while the main review object is methodological/epistemological knowledge co-production across all water environments (including Arctic sea ice, marine planning, fish/forests, and watersheds).
